title: The Sicilian Dragon
description: An easy-to-learn and easy-to-play variation of the legendary Sicilian Defense, relying on Black's dark squared bishop on g7.

2r2rk1/pp1bp1bp/3p1npB/q3n3/3NP1P1/2N2P2.text:
White might sense blood in the water and go for the trade now.

But this is incorrect.

We'll take.

2r2rk1/pp1bp2p/3p1npQ/q3n3/3NP1P1/2N2P2/.text:
So that the queen arrives on h7.

Our knight is guarding the h7-square for now, and there is no danger.

Which means we can sacrifice on c3!

2r2rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1nP1/q3n3/3NP1P1/2N1BP.text:
White could disregard our expansion completely and just capture on g6.

The correct recapture is with the f-pawn. That allows our f8-rook to join the defense on f7 if needed.  

And if White's queen leaves the post on d2, we can actually infiltrate with the exchange sacrifice on c3.

2r2rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q3n2P/3NP1P1/2N1B.text:
Kb1 is a very natural move to slide the king away from the rook on c8 as well as defend the a2-pawn. 

However, this allows us to spring our powerful trap, and that's to take on f3 with the knight!

The idea is to unleash the powerful bishop on g7 and remove the guard of e4 and g4.

For the price of the knight, White will find it extremely hard to defend all the targets, as you will see.

2r2rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q6P/4P1P1/2N1BN2/.text:
But when White captures on f3, that's not all.

We can implement a standard and thematic exchange sacrifice here!

Now sacrificing a whole rook, we want the c3-pawn to eventually be a target for the knight.

You are about to see how well this position works for us tactically.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/6P1/3NP3/2N1BP2.text: Pushing the g-pawn all the way is the wrong approach for White.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP1PP/2N1BP2.text:
White continues pushing, unbothered.

The pawn is coming to h5, but we can still afford to play in the center.

And we'll place the knight on e5. It pressures the f3-square from there and wants to jump to c4.

It seems like White is much quicker with their attack...

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np2p1/6Pn/3NP3/2N1BP2/.text:
After ...Nh5, their attack is blocked.

This is not the way to play for White.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/4n2P/3NP1P1/2N1B.text:
Especially when they play h5, already chipping away at our structure, which is what Study 1 is about.

It's played two thirds of the time.

But we have ...Qa5!

From the a5-square, the queen is pressuring both the knight on c3 and the pawn on a2.

5rk1/pp1bp2p/3p1npQ/4n3/3NP1P1/2q2P2/P1P.text:
And now our queen comes in, with the threat of ...Qa1+.

The position is still equal according to the computer but one little slip might decide the game in an unstable position like this.

White's best move is probably Kb1 after which we can go for ...b5.

5rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/7P/4P1P1/2P1BN2/P1P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

Now that we set everything up the way we wanted, it's time to gobble up the pawns.

5rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q6P/4P1P1/2Q1BN2/PP.text:
White captures with the queen.

Since they're up material, they want to trade as much as possible.

Which is fine.

We counted on it.

5rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/7P/4P1b1/2P1BN2/P1P5.text:
First, we'll capture on g4, pinning the knight and threatening to take with a fork.

If White plays Be2, we can capture on e4 and threaten multiple forks.

If White tries to go for Bd4 at some point, ...e5 is a good move to keep the momentum.

We'll have a lot of pawns and plenty of compensation for the rook.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
And they do.

The main line for Black is actually 9...d5 here, striking in the center, but I recommend developing with ...Bd7.

It could be considered a bit risky because we take some time to get all the pieces out.

However, it's also an option that gives us a straightforward attacking plan and a brilliant trap many players fall into.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP1P1/2N1BP2.text:
Meanwhile, White starts the kingside operations.

Here, g4 is played over 40% of the time. White's idea is simple: h4 and h5.

To counter that, we are going to play on the queenside.

Next, a good plan would be to try and get the knight to c4 to target White's key attackers.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text:
White goes ahead with their plan and creates the bishop and queen battery 80% of the time.

This also prepares queenside castling.

After ...Nc6, our intention is not to trade on d4 but to slowly improve our position and wait for White to commit to castling.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PPP.text:
Which is why White usually plays f3.

We'll castle kingside, and activate the queenside pieces next.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
White could choose to reply with a number of different moves, but we will stick to the most common ones and the main line in Chapter 1.

Be3 is played 35% of the time, in almost 2.5 million games!

The idea behind Be3 is to play Qd2 in the future and try to trade off the dark-squared bishops.

We will fianchetto either way, threatening ...Ng4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White defends by bringing the knight to c3.

This is the famous starting position in the Sicilian.

We'll fianchetto. The pawn structure often prompts White to castle long and attack our king.

On the other hand, once White does castle long, our bishop on g7 becomes one of the most important pieces.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White activates the knight.

This move prepares d4 anyway, which is fine as we want to trade when that pawn arrives in the center.

We will create the pawn chain on the dark squares, keeping our structure and our central presence solid.

This blocks the dark-squared bishop but we will activate it to g7 in the Dragon.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White advances in the center.

Allowing them to keep both pawns there would be giving them too much power.

So we will capture.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
The knight recaptures.

Time to start piece development.

The knight on f6 attacks the central e4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our course on the Sicilian Dragon.

The Dragon is one of the most popular variations of the Sicilian where we play on the dark squares in the center, but fianchetto the dark-squared bishop early.

The main line is famous and long, and players usually castle on opposite sides, making the Dragon known for sharp, tactical and aggressive battles!

2r1b1k1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/2P1BP2.text:
A nice move to remember is ...Be8!

We want to free the d7-square for the knight which can become one of our main attacking pieces.

It's coming to b6, and then to c4 or a4.

White will certainly have to react to our moves for a while without thinking about attacking themselves at all.

2r2r1k/pp1bNpbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/4BP2/P.text:
Which doesn't give them time to take our rook on c8.

We've lost a pawn so far, but that's not all.

The knight is now under attack and there are only two moves that don't lose the game for White on the spot, which are g5 and h5.

But even if White knows the theory here, they are also tricky and give us some advantage.

2r2rk1/pp1bNpbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/4BP2/P.text:
Well, White's idea is that they have an intermezzo on e7.

But they would have to be extremely accurate not to lose the game here, which I doubt many players will.

We'll evade the check, and now White has to recapture the queen first.

2r2rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q2Nn3/3NP1PP/4BP2.text:
Now that the a2-pawn is defended, they want to move the knight to the center and offer a queen trade.

This is usually a trick we need to watch out for when White plays Kb1, but here White is the one getting tricked!

We'll take. What is this trick about?

2r2rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q3n3/3NP1PP/2N1BP.text:
This isn't winning for us or anything, but the Dragon is so sharp that often the side that's allowed to attack first wins.

And we will definitely put some pressure on White's position now by sacrificing the rook on c3!

Even at the price of trading queens, giving up the rook for the knight on c3 allows us to exploit White's key weaknesses down the line.

2r3k1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/2P1BP2/.text: The king can defend, but we're not done applying pressure.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP1PP/2N1BP2.text:
White pushes the h-pawn as well.

While our knight begins its journey in the center.

The last study showed the aggressive 12.h5.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/2N1BP.text:
White might play the prophylactic Kb1 on move 12, which is done about 10% of the time.

This could become a tricky line.

We'll play ...Qa5 to attack the knight and threaten the sacrifice as in the main line.

But White played Kb1 for a reason.

In order to avoid our ...Nxf3 trap in the future, White has to know this key idea, placing the bishop on e2.

This move is played 17% of the time.

It does solve that problem for White but gives us the momentum to play aggressive moves.

One of them is placing the queen on a5. White could go on the defensive here.

4rr1k/pp1b1pbp/3p1np1/3Nn3/3NP1PP/4BP2/P.text:
If they play the natural Nd5 instead, it's over.

We'll take the knight.

4rr1k/pp1b1pbp/3p2p1/3P4/6PP/4BN2/PPPR4/.text: So they have to take on f3.

4rr1k/pp1b1pbp/3p2p1/3Pn3/3N2PP/4BP2/PPP.text:
The pawn has to recapture, and the crucial aspect of the position is the undefended bishop on e3.

There's a tactic here.

We can capture on f3 and we are infiltrating.

5r1k/pp1b1pbp/3p2p1/3P4/6PP/4rN2/PPPR4/1.text:
But now the bishop falls and the knight on f3 is under attack, as well as the pawn on g4.

We will be up a pawn with a bishop pair, controlling the only open file in the position.

Black is winning.

5rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/4n3/3NP1PP/2P1BP2/P.text:
Now White has some serious targets around the king.

Which we will begin to attack immediately.

White's weak pawns and the exposed king are what provides compensation for the sacrifice and the queen trade.

5rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/q3n3/3NP1PP/2Q1BP2/.text:
The queen takes.

Trading queens is fine.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
White finally castles.

And we will go with our usual plan of ...Bd7.

The rook is coming to the c-file and the knight is coming to the center.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP1P1/2N1BP2.text:
The most standard is White beginning to advance their pawns in this position.

Which we don't have to be afraid of yet.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text:
White lines up the queen with the bishop and prepares castling.

And we'll activate the knight to the best square.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PPP.text:
White stops ...Ng4 now.

And we'll castle, having developed the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
White goes for the main Be3.

Keep in mind that ...Ng4 here loses to Bb5+.

So we will fianchetto first.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Developing the knight and preparing d4.

We'll strengthen our pawn chain.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White advances in the center.

It's best to capture.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll attack the pawn in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will deal with some alternatives for White on move 12, such as 12.Be2 and 12.Kb1.

White moving the bishop to e2 might suggest they know about our trap from Study 1 and want to stop it.

On the other hand, 12.Kb1 often leads to sharp lines where we are the ones who can come out on top!

2rq1rk1/pp1bppb1/2np1np1/7p/3NP2P/2N1BP2.text:
We'll continue with our standard ideas.

The knight is coming to the center and our queen will join the queenside.

I would say this is more favorable for us than 10.g4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
Opposite side castling usually signifies a fierce battle to come.

Let's develop the bishop with the standard ideas and await White's next move.

One of the ideas is Kb1, which transposes.

Another option is Bc4 but placing the bishop on the c-file plays into our pieces.

r2q1r2/pp1bppkp/3p1np1/8/4P3/2N2P2/PPPQ3.text:
And after we take, our kingside is intact and we've won a clean pawn.

White doesn't have an attack and we'll go for the usual ...Rc8 and ...Qa5.

The queen could even go to b6.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppBp/3p1np1/8/3nP3/2N2P2/PPP.text:
White has to take on g7 first.

But now we have an intermezzo.

We can capture on f3 and attack the queen!

r2q1rk1/pp1bppb1/2np1np1/7p/3NP2P/2N1BP2.text:
Instead, they can activate the bishop and perhaps prepare for g4 to come in the future.

But this is already much slower than g4 right away.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP2P/2N1BP2/.text:
White starts with h4 first just over 15% of the time.

We can play ...Rc8 here and the positions will likely transpose to lines we've already covered after g4.

However, there is an additional option. Since White hasn't played g4, we can try to block the attack!

White shouldn't go crazy here with g4 and h5 attempts.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1npB/8/3NP3/2N2P2/PP.text:
When going through the main line, I mentioned that White's general idea with Be3 and Qd2 is to try and trade off the bishops on h6 at some point.

In this position, it's a mistake, though. It's too early and fails due a tactical combination from our side.

We can capture on d4 and force White's hand!

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text:
White prepares castling as well.

And we'll develop the knight to the active c6-square.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
White activates the dark-squared bishop.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White defends.

Let's go for the Dragon Sicilian.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Activating the knight.

We'll reinforce the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White advances with d4.

Let's take.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
The knight recaptures.

Time to develop and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Let's focus on White's deviations from the main line with 10.g4.

In particular, these include White attacking with the h-pawn first or going for the exchange on h6 immediately.

Both of these moves could be considered suboptimal as we have solutions for each of them.

2r2r2/3bppkp/3p2p1/q2P4/1p1Q3P/1B3P2/1PP.text:
Because White has a check on d4.

We'll slide back to g8.

2r2rk1/3bpp1p/3p2p1/q2P3P/1p1Q4/1B3P2/1P.text:
White might think they're the one attacking after h5.

But it's not that simple.

2r2rk1/3bppbp/3p2p1/q2B4/1p1BP2P/5P2/1PP.text:
Sliding the king to b1 doesn't work.

Do you see a powerful sacrifice?

We need a rook on a8. But one rook is enough!

2r2rk1/4pp1p/3p2p1/q2P1b1P/1p1Q4/1B3P2/1.text:
We still have the light-squared bishop, and we're threatening to capture on c2 and then push ...b3.

This combination could be devastating for White if they allow it.

2rq1r2/3bppkp/3p2p1/3P4/1p5P/1B3P2/1PPQ2.text:
Now White trades in the center.

We can bring the queen to a5, but it is not as dangerous anymore.

2rq1rk1/3b1pb1/3p2p1/3B1p2/pp2P3/5P2/PPP.text:
We'll recapture on g6 and we should be getting to White's king first with the a- and b-pawns.

White isn't that quick with the attack.

Our rook and bishop on g7 are already pressuring the key weak spots around the king and our queen will be joining them soon.

2rq1rk1/3b1pbp/3p1np1/1p1Bp2P/p3P3/2N1BP.text:
This is important because it avoids any trades, further restricts White's space and keeps the momentum going.

Now we can attack the knight as well.

2rq1rk1/3b1pbp/3p1np1/3Bp2P/pp2P3/4BP2/P.text:
White retreats to e2.

Another reason behind Bxf6 being necessary before Bd5 is that we can use our knight to trade on d5 now.

And White has to recapture with the queen to try and keep hold of the game.

However, even that looks extremely weak after ...Qc7.

2rq1rk1/3b1pbp/3p1pp1/1p1B3P/p3P3/2N2P2/.text:
So they slide to d5.

They won't be capturing our d6-pawn any time soon.

Meanwhile, we can continue harassing them with ...b4.

2rq1rk1/3b1pbp/3p1pp1/3B3P/pp2P3/5P2/PPP.text:
The knight retreats to e2, and now our pawns are pretty far advanced.

But let's take a move to play something else first.

We need to open up our bishop.

2rq1rk1/3b1pbp/3p2p1/3Pp2P/pp6/4BP2/PPPQ.text: But if White captures with the pawn, it's over.

2rq1rk1/3bppBp/3p2p1/3n4/1p2P2P/1B3P2/1P.text:
Capturing on g7 keeps the position in the balance.

If we go for ...Qa5, White has the amazing Qh6.

Let's just recapture instead.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1Bp1/1p5P/p3P3/1BN2P2/P.text:
Capturing on f6 is not a blunder, but giving up the bishop like this isn't the best from a positional standpoint.

Still, it's probably the best move according to the computer because there aren't many good alternatives.

We'll gladly take and look to push ...f5 at some point. This hangs the d6-pawn, but White's bishop is still under attack.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/1p1B3P/p2BP3/2N2P2.text:
White could escape to d5 here, but that's a mistake when they don't take on f6 first.

Because we have this cheeky ...e5 idea.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/3N4/1p1BP2P/1B3P2/.text:
They have to jump to either d5 or a2.

And d5 is the more active square to try and trade off some pieces.

We'll capture on d5, opening up our bishop.

White has a choice between capturing the bishop on g7 or the knight on d5. One of the captures loses.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/p7/1P1BP2P/1BN2P2/.text:
White captures.

But we keep a pawn on b4.

If White isn't careful now and plays something like Ne2, there could be ...Qa5 ideas in the near future.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/p7/N2BP2P/1B3P2/1P.text:
White recaptures with the knight first.

We'll trade again.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/pp5P/3BP3/1BN2P2/P.text:
White declares war with h5.

Let's see who is faster.

We'll attack the bishop.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/pp6/3BP2P/PBN2P2/1.text:
A more reasonable defensive move than a4 is definitely a3.

White doesn't commit to tactical sequences but rather takes away the b4-square.

Or do they? We will still play ...b4!

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p1np1/pp6/P2BP2P/1BN2P2/.text:
The second most popular move in the position is a4, and it loses the game!

We've got a forcing combination.

Let's take on a4.

2rq1rk1/3bppbp/3p2p1/3B4/1p1BP2P/5P2/1PP.text:
Capturing on d5 loses the game on the spot.

Due to an idea I already mentioned, ...Qa5.

We are threatening checkmate in one and it's actually not easy to stop it.

2rq1rk1/4ppbp/3p1np1/p7/B2BP2P/5P2/1PPQ2.text:
Why did we make these trades?

Because we've got a fork on c4!

2rq1rk1/5pbp/3p2p1/3Ppb1P/pp6/4BP2/PPPQN.text:
We can target the c2-pawn with
and there's no Nd4 for White to defend with thanks to our ...e5 idea.

There are no defensive moves other than that.

A move like c3 will prove not to work eventually. We're winning.

2rq1rk1/p2bppbp/3p1np1/1p6/3BP2P/1BN2P2/.text:
They can try to counterattack on the kingside.

The position is still equal according to the computer, but remember that whoever strikes first might just win.

In that spirit, we'll continue pushing.

White can either choose to react to our attack here or continue attempting to attack themselves.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/1BN1BP2/.text: We'll bring the rook to the active c-file anyway and look to rotate the knight to either c4 or capture the bishop on b3.

They retreat to b3.

Now, we could go for the standard ...Ne5 and ...Nc4 idea, but I propose something else.

Let's capture on d4, relieve some tension and open up the rook.

Instead of going the slower and positional route, let's attack on the queenside as soon as possible.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/8/3BP3/1BN2P2/PP.text:
White recaptures.

And now we can push ...b5 with the idea of a pawn storm on the queenside.

Our rook is already on the perfect square and our queen is waiting to join.

In fact, White has scored poorly in practice from this position because our attack is much quicker, simpler and direct.

3q1rk1/4ppbp/3p1np1/p7/2rBP2P/1B3P2/1PPQ.text: But what's our idea? White can simply retreat to b3.

3q1rk1/4ppbp/3p2p1/p7/2rBn2P/1B3P2/1PPQ2.text:
We can capture on e4!

White's queen is under attack so they don't have time to capture the rook on c4.

And if they capture the knight on e4, we will take the bishop on d4!

This is extremely strong for us because we can bring the rook back to b4 at some point and play ...a4, with the bishop on g7 now being a monster.

B4rk1/3bppbp/3p2p1/q7/1p1BP2P/5P2/1PPQ2P.text:
White captures.

And we'll recapture on a8.

The queen is coming.

r1b2rk1/pp2pp1p/1qnp2p1/8/3BP1P1/1BN5/PP.text:
White captures.

And we'll force a trade of queens,
too.

White is not going to be able to defend as easily without the queens on the board.

r1b2rk1/pp2pp1p/2np2p1/3N4/4P1P1/1B6/PPP.text:
Let's fall back and protect the pawn instead.

Our bishop is coming to e6 next and we can play ...Kg7 to improve the king for the endgame and unpin the f7-pawn.

We will play against White's weak pawns in the long run.

r1b2rk1/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/3N4/3nP1P1/1B6/PPP.text:
And now the knight comes in to attack the e7-pawn.

We don't have to trade on b3 as well and open up White's rook.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/1qnp1np1/8/3NP3/1BN1BP2/.text:
Once White defends, we have a tactic. The queen is also placed on the critical dark-squared diagonal.

We can play ...Ng4 with a discovered attack on the knight on d4!

White's options are limited here because we are also attacking the bishop on e3.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/1qnp2p1/8/3NP1P1/1BN1B3/.text:

White develops the bishop.

But we create more tension in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White opens up the rook to go ahead with their plan.

Sure enough, the e4-pawn is defended and they are aiming for d4.

How to stop it? We will play ...e5!

Even though we block our own bishop, we need to take as much control of d4 as possible.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3p1np1/2p1p3/3PP3/2P2N2/.text:
They can still play d4, but it's different now.

We'll take with the c-pawn first, although it makes no difference.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3p1np1/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
Because we will capture with both pawns anyway.

Now White won't be able to keep a pawn on d4.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/8/PP3PPP/R.text: They get the knight to it instead.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1.text:
White centralizes the rook.

They want to defend the e4-pawn with it and then play d4.

But we won't make it that easy for them.

Let's get the king out of the way first.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White castles.

And we'll fianchetto, also ready to castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2p5/4P3/2PP1N2/P.text:
We'll simply play ...g6, Dragon style.

What's crucial about this variation is that we want to play ...e5 and completely lock down the d4-square, disallowing White from ever playing it if they haven't already.

When we lock down the center, we will feel much more comfortable about advancing on a side of the board, like with ...b5 and ...b4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1.text:
They develop the light-squared bishop instead.

Let's go for a Dragon-like approach, with ...g6.

You know where the bishop is going.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2PP1N2/PP.text:
White could switch their plans and go for d3 here.

The pawn structure looks passive and unnecessary but is solid.

Although White has given up on any opportunity to be the offensive side.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight comes out to f3.

We'll strengthen the pawns.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
3.Bb5+ is played only 6% of the time, and it gives us a healthy position and a lot of central space in the long run.

There is no advantage in White trading the light-squared bishops early.

We'll block with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
When you see White going for a setup with the two knights, this is what you should think about.

Nc3 on move 3 is played 8% of the time.

They haven't used the chance to play d4, so why shouldn't we control it with additional pieces when we can?

That's when developing the knight to c6 first becomes logical.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P1.text:
White going for c3 on move 2 or 3 is called the Alapin Sicilian, and you should face it around 10% of the time. It's been played in more than 8.5 million games.

White wants d4, but the e4-pawn is now weaker as the c3-square is occupied by the pawn.

Still, we need to be careful in this position. We aren't actually attacking the pawn because if we were to capture it, White would have the fork on a4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The final study will show further examples of early deviations by White, specifically on move 3.

This includes 3.c3, 3.Nc3 and 3.Bb5+.

Our setups will certainly have to change depending on what White plays, so let's see how our Dragon approach works here.
